source.title: From Symmetry to Invariance: Learning Galois Equivalent Representations in Finite Fields

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and symbols are imperfectly rendered in the text extraction, but the prose and reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses grokking as background and studies transfer of finite-field multiplication across equivalent basis representations. It does not test delayed generalization after training accuracy saturates, gradual circuit formation, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extensive results on transfer among equivalent representations, but its test bases share multiplication rules with training bases. It does not report the delayed train/test accuracy pattern named in the claim; its grokking discussion is background rather than a tested result. Related representation-transfer findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: Grokking is introduced only as background, citing Power et al. and Nanda et al. The experiments test transfer of finite-field multiplication across Galois-equivalent basis representations, and every held-out rule also appears in training. No result addresses delayed generalization, its dependence on training-set size, circuit formation, training regime, LLMs, weight decay, algorithm identity across runs, or optimizer artifacts. The study gives no grokking-style data fraction or weight-decay sweep. Its training is short (50 to 800 epochs with Adam), so late generalization could not be observed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that learning an algebraic operation and transferring it across equivalent representations are distinct problems. In F8, orbit labels and a learned Galois action combined with deterministic canonicalization give strong transfer. The constructive procedures are less reliable in F16, where accurate transformation learning is the bottleneck.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains on complete finite-field multiplication tables and tests transfer across Galois-equivalent basis representations. It does not reproduce the original grokking setup or measure delayed generalization after overfitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer outcomes vary with the information and objective provided to the model, field size, and experimental seed. In F8, adding basis tokens to the orbit label yields variable results; in F16, learned transformation and canonicalization are less reliable.

fits_no_version.finding: In F8, explicit orbit labels give perfect held-out multiplication. Pairwise orbit recognition transfers above chance while direct orbit identification stays at chance. A learned Frobenius transformation gives near-perfect canonicalization and downstream multiplication.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small Transformers can transfer finite-field multiplication across held-out basis representations when given orbit information, or when a learned Galois transformation is used to build canonical identifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: In F16, pairwise recognition stays strong and direct identification is above chance but well below training accuracy. Learned transformation and canonicalization are less reliable than in F8, while ground-truth canonicalization still supports accurate multiplication.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transfer across equivalent finite-field basis representations becomes less reliable as the field grows, and is limited by how accurately the transformation is learned.

fits_no_version.finding: The decomposed matrix-vector plus reference-basis pipeline transfers to held-out transformations strongly in F8, with seed variation, and very unevenly in F16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Separately learned algebraic modules can compose to support multiplication on held-out basis representations, with reliability depending on field size and run.

record.problems: The paper's test sets contain held-out bases from Galois orbits represented during training, so they do not test unseen multiplication rules. Results in several conditions vary substantially across seeds. The F16 experiments use a fixed sample of 50 orbits rather than exhaustive coverage.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; 17 selected rows cover the reported transfer outcomes relevant as related findings. Other condition-specific multiplication controls and secondary approximate-recovery results are not included because they do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No delayed rise in held-out accuracy after training saturation is reported or sought. No training-set-size sweep. Orbit identification stays near chance through 300 epochs, but this is not a grokking-style split and training is short.
No mechanistic analysis of learned circuits or progress measures.
No non-algorithmic data, and no sweep of initialization scale or weight norm.
No weight-decay manipulation, critical dataset size, or ungrokking test. One F8 run drops from high accuracy back to the floor, but this is not tied to dataset size or norm.
Internal algorithms are not compared across runs. Seed variation is reported only in accuracy.
No test of optimizer or numerical-precision artifacts.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are correctly linked to no version. r16 is a ground-truth canonicalization comparator, not a learned result. r2 and r3 sit at the modal baseline of 0.3438, not at chance. Several curves show train/held-out gaps that are never closed, for example F16 Galois action: training exact 1.0 within about 20 epochs, held-out exact 0.22 to 0.44. These are not evidence against V1, because the setup, optimizer (Adam, no weight decay stated) and training lengths are not grokking protocols.

versions.untested_parts: No test of chance-level test accuracy after training saturation followed by a delayed rise, or of delay increasing as the training set shrinks.
No mechanistic analysis of a generalizing arithmetic circuit forming gradually, memorizing components being removed, or progress measures anticipating a grokking jump.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning.
No test of weight decay or low-norm bias as an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The paper does not identify and compare internal algorithms learned across runs to test whether they converge to the same algorithm.
No test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities, floating-point softmax limits, or whether controlling such artifacts removes grokking.
